extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, critics, and public speakers; cultivated readers interested in literary taste and rhetoric (early-18th-century polite audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and prescriptive rules for recognising, cultivating, and exercising 'fine taste' in writing and rhetoric, plus related guidance on oratory, translation, and the use of music in devotional drama. Geared toward authors, critics, and public speakers seeking to improve style and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine Taste (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine Taste: 'that Faculty of the Soul, which discerns the Beauties of an Author with Pleasure, and the Imperfections with Dislike.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via the metaphor of gustatory sense: there are degrees of refinement; a person of fine taste discerns not only general beauties but the most concealed faults and nicest perfections in writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for possessing fine taste
rubrics_metrics.description: If upon perusal of the celebrated Works of Antiquity or those Moderns sanctioned by polite contemporaries one is not extraordinarily delighted, or feels coldness at admired passages, one lacks the faculty of fine taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the classics and highly regarded moderns—if they fail to move you, the defect is in the reader, not necessarily the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discern the specifick qualities of authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to 'taste the distinguishing Perfections, or ... the Specifick Qualities of the Author' (e.g., Livy's manner of telling a story; Sallust's entry into internal principles; Tacitus's display of outward motives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A refined reader should identify which particular excellences of style or thought distinguish one author from another, including foreign infusions and borrowings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise how expression alters apprehension of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: There is as much difference in apprehending a Thought clothed in Cicero's Language and that of a common Author as in seeing by taper-light vs sunlight; fine taste discerns this difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess not only ideas but the manner of expression; great diction can transform the same idea into a higher pleasure or impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate taste by conversance with polished authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Be conversant among the writings of the most polite Authors; repeated reading reveals new beauties and naturally wears one into a similar manner of speaking and thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent, attentive reading of masterly works is the most natural method to improve one's faculty of taste and to internalize polished expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve taste through conversation with men of polite genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversation with men of a polite Genius furnishes reflections and hints not produced by solitary reading and helps one perceive aspects of authors one might miss alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogues with accomplished peers broaden perception; many great writers appear in groups of contemporaries influenced by mutual discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the best critics—beyond mechanical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Be well versed in the works of the best Criticks, Ancient and Modern; critics ought to 'enter into the very Spirit and Soul of fine Writing' rather than only mechanical rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek critics who explain the deeper sources of pleasure in literature (Longinus is cited as exemplary); avoid critics who restrict themselves to surface rules like unities without probing imaginative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the 'Gothic' taste: avoid forced conceits and mere epigrams
rubrics_metrics.description: The English general taste for Epigram, Turns of Wit, and forced Conceits are false kinds which 'have no manner of Influence, either for the bettering or enlarging the Mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for natural simplicity of thought; banish contrived conceits and cleverness that does not enrich or enlarge the reader's mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratory: study proper gesture and vehement voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper Gestures and vehement Exertions of the Voice cannot be too much studied by a public Orator: they comment on what he utters, enforce it, keep the Audience awake, and show he is in earnest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe the examples of celebrated Greek and Latin orators; gestures and vocal force can move even ignorant audiences. But be wary: excessive or ill-bred gestures (pocket-fumbling, hat-moulding, absurd mannerisms) are ridiculous and can undermine authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratory: either eschew gestures or make them graceful
rubrics_metrics.description: Either lay aside all kinds of Gesture (if that suits national genius) or at least make use only of gestures that are graceful and expressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt aimless or vulgar physical habits while speaking; choose a coherent physical style—either restrained or cultivated and expressive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Musick in religious drama and worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Music, when applied to religious worship or the early chorus-form of drama, 'raises noble Hints in the Mind of the Hearer... strengthens Devotion, and advances Praise into Rapture' producing more lasting impressions than ordinary words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chorus originally served to mark vice and recommend virtue; musical entertainments purify and exalt passions and cherish divine impulses—so musical elements in devotional or dramatic contexts should aim at these moral and affective ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance for translating songs/poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating pastoral/love songs (example: Scheffer's Song), keep the 'pretty Images of Rural Nature' and naturally interweave the circumstances of the journey, anxiety of absence, gloominess of roads, resolution regarding routes, impatience at slow travel, and joyful surprise at the mistress's appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If some images are lost in imitation, allow the translation to 'supply the Place of a long Letter' but avoid displacing any single line of the original author's superior hand; preserve naturalness and the emotional sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good writing: examine human nature and trace passions to causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Human Nature is the most useful object of reason; by observing the nature and course of Passions we can trace every Action from its first Conception to its Death—good writing explains motives (jealousy, ambition, etc.) and connects passion to action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should use reason to adjust passions but not aim to eradicate them; literature that maps passion -> action clarifies behaviour and improves moral understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance passion and reason in composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions are necessary to move and animate the understanding (they 'put it in Motion'); but they must be kept under the command of Reason—govern them like free subjects, not slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid both extremes: neither extinguish passion through excessive severity nor let unruly passions override reason. Cultivate passions to preserve vigour without surrendering moral or intellectual control.
